statement: In 62 people recruited by staff of six US overdose-training and naloxone-distribution programmes in 2005–2006 (in Chicago, New Mexico, San Francisco, Baltimore and two in New York City; 72.6% men, 85.5% currently or formerly using drugs, 22.6% syringe-exchange staff), the 30 trained by the recruiting programme (a median of 8 months before, range 1 to 80 months) compared with the 32 not trained by it were associated with higher scores at recognising opioid overdoses in 16 written scenarios and at deciding when naloxone was called for, scored against the answers of 11 medical experts; trained people still misjudged some opioid overdoses, and both groups often misjudged the scenarios that were not opioid overdoses. The scenarios were experiences that people who inject drugs had described as overdoses in an earlier study; by the experts' combined answers, 9 were opioid overdoses, all calling for naloxone, and 7 were non-opioid overdoses or not overdoses, not calling for it, and respondents could also answer that there was not enough information. Trained respondents recognised on average 7.13 of the 9 opioid overdoses (SD 1.38) against 5.18 (SD 2.55) for untrained respondents (p < 0.001), but 4.63 against 4.28 of the 7 other scenarios (p = 0.42); their totals, 11.77 against 9.47 of 16 (p < 0.005), are 73.6% and 59.2% correct (editors' calculation), not the 85.2% and 68.3% printed in the paper's table and text. Trained respondents chose naloxone in 6.93 of the 9 opioid overdoses against 5.77 (p < 0.05), so on average they did not choose it in about 2 of the 9 against about 3 (2.1 and 3.2 in the paper), and chose it in 0.4 against 1.7 of the 7 scenarios where it was not called for (p < 0.001); naloxone totals were 13.53 against 11.09 of 16 (84.6% and 69.3% correct, p < 0.0001). The experts themselves answered that there was not enough information in 25.6% of their ratings, against 16.0% for trained respondents. The paper reports agreement with the experts as a weighted kappa of 0.85 (95% CI 0.72 to 0.98) for trained and 0.48 (0.18 to 0.77) for untrained respondents, and a kappa of 1.0 for trained respondents' naloxone choices, without saying what was compared; since trained individuals averaged 84.6% correct on naloxone, these figures cannot mean that each trained person matched the experts. All six programmes taught how to tell an opioid overdose from a 'heavy nod', and two explicitly covered non-opioid (for example stimulant) overdoses. The paper gives no results by scenario or by sign and does not print the scenarios, so it cannot show which situations, a heavy nod among them, people got wrong. Programme staff chose who took part and nobody was tested before training, so the difference cannot be credited to training; two of the 11 experts who set the answers are named among the evaluated programmes' staff; the scenarios were written descriptions, not real overdoses; and the paper does not mention fentanyl. The authors' conclusion that 'naloxone training programs are effective and probably cost–effective' rests on this one comparison, with no costs, deaths or real overdoses measured (Green et al., 2008). Whether take-home naloxone programmes lower deaths is a separate answer (see the answer on naloxone programmes). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Would you know if someone was overdosing on opioids? Not always, in the one study read, which used written stories rather than real overdoses. In 2005–2006, staff at six US overdose programmes asked 62 people, most of whom used or had used drugs, to judge 16 short written descriptions of experiences that people who inject drugs had called an overdose; 11 medical experts had decided that 9 were opioid overdoses needing naloxone and 7 were not. People the programmes had trained spotted on average about 7 of the 9 opioid overdoses, and people they had not trained about 5. Trained people still did not choose naloxone in about 2 of the 9 (untrained people about 3), and both groups got only about 4 or 5 of the other 7 right. The experts themselves said there was not enough information in about a quarter of their answers. Staff chose who took part, nobody was tested before training, and the paper does not say which descriptions people got wrong. So it cannot show whether training caused the difference, which signs people miss, or whether people could tell a heavy nod from an overdose, which all six programmes taught.
population: People recruited by staff at six US overdose-training and naloxone-distribution programmes (Chicago; State of New Mexico; San Francisco; Baltimore; New York City, two programmes), October 2005 to July 2006: 62 respondents, 72.6% men, 85.5% currently or formerly using drugs, 22.6% syringe-exchange staff
exposure: Having been trained in overdose recognition and response by the recruiting programme (a median of 8 months before; trainings of about 15 to 120 minutes)
comparator: People at the same programmes not trained by them (32); and an answer key from 11 medical experts combined by latent class analysis
outcome: Number of 16 written overdose scenarios correctly classified (opioid overdose, or non-opioid overdose or not an overdose) and correctly judged as calling or not calling for naloxone; agreement with the experts (kappa)
magnitude: Green et al. (2008), trained (n = 30) against untrained (n = 32), mean (SD): opioid overdoses recognised 7.13 (1.38) against 5.18 (2.55) of 9, t60 = −3.76, P < 0.001; other scenarios 4.63 (1.40) against 4.28 (1.94) of 7, P = 0.42; recognition total 11.77 (1.92) against 9.47 (3.48) of 16, P < 0.005 (73.6% against 59.2%, editors' calculation; printed as 85.2% against 68.3%); naloxone chosen in opioid overdoses 6.93 (1.76) against 5.77 (2.30) of 9, P < 0.05 (not chosen in 2.1 against 3.2); naloxone correctly not chosen 6.60 (0.72) against 5.32 (1.94) of 7, P < 0.001 (chosen where not called for in 0.4 against 1.7); naloxone total 13.53 (1.96) against 11.09 (2.32) of 16 (84.6% against 69.3%), P < 0.0001. 'Not enough information' in 25.6% of the experts' ratings against 16.0% of trained respondents'. Weighted kappa with the experts 0.85 (0.72–0.98) trained, 0.48 (0.18–0.77) untrained; naloxone kappa 1.0 trained, 0.75 (0.44–1.0) untrained (unit of comparison not stated).

evidence.extracted: Staff of six overdose-training and naloxone-distribution programmes (Chicago; State of New Mexico; San Francisco; Baltimore; New York City: Citiwide and Positive Health Project), approached at a national conference, were each asked to recruit five people trained and five not trained by their programme, at sites where people who use or used drugs gather; participants were paid $10 and completed a paper questionnaire on their own, with site staff available for questions or to administer it when literacy was a problem. 62 took part between October 2005 and July 2006: 30 trained (a median of 8 months before, range 1–80 months) and 32 untrained (three trained elsewhere, counted as untrained); 72.6% men, 85.5% currently or formerly using drugs, 22.6% syringe-exchange staff (needle-exchange employees were 30.0% of the trained and 15.6% of the untrained).

evidence.extracted: The 16 scenarios were experiences that people who inject drugs had described as overdoses, chosen from 60 reported in a study of public injecting; development and validation are reported elsewhere (a 2006 conference abstract). Eleven medical experts classified each as opioid overdose, non-opioid overdose, not an overdose, or not enough information/unsure, and said whether naloxone was indicated; with the non-opioid and non-overdose categories collapsed, latent class analysis of their answers gave the key: 9 opioid overdoses, all requiring naloxone, and 7 non-opioid or non-overdose scenarios, not requiring it. Recognition and naloxone scores each ranged from 0 to 16. No data were gathered on age, race, ethnicity or drugs used. The scenario texts are not printed.

evidence.extracted: The Discussion says training programmes improved recognition and response significantly, and that the study gives key evidence, without a large multi-site study or a cost-effectiveness analysis, that the programmes are effective and probably cost-effective. Limitations stated: small sample and insufficient power for site differences; an observational design open to self-report and reporting bias; non-random recruitment at each site; residual confounding from limited demographic data. The Acknowledgements name Sharon Stancliff and Bernie Lieving both among the staff of the evaluation sites and among the 11 medical experts.

evidence.quote: naloxone training programs are effective and probably cost–effective

risk_of_bias.note: A single cross-sectional comparison of groups chosen by programme staff, with no scores before training and no measure of motivation, earlier knowledge, age or drug use; the outcome is answers to unpublished written scenarios, scored against a key partly set by experts who are also programme staff, and staff who knew who was trained could help people fill in the questionnaire (card sc_green_2008: ROBINS-I serious).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: written scenarios, 2005–2006, people recruited at harm-reduction programmes. As an answer about recognising a real overdose today, fentanyl included, it would be rated lower still, which the statement says; the rating is already at its floor.

imprecision.note: 30 and 32 people, but the differences in opioid recognition and in the naloxone totals are large against their spread (P < 0.001 and P < 0.0001); the difference in naloxone choices for the 9 opioid overdoses alone is less precise (P < 0.05).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; no protocol or registration.

grade.reasoning: Observational (a non-randomized comparison of trained and untrained people at one time): starts low; risk of bias −1 (see the domain note); inconsistency, indirectness as worded, imprecision and publication bias 0. Very low. Status single study: no other study of how well people recognise overdose scenarios was read. The claim is worded as an association between having been trained and scores on written scenarios; whether training causes better recognition, how people do at real overdoses, which signs they miss and whether training changes deaths or costs are not shown by this design. The paper's printed recognition percentages do not match its means, and its kappa of 1.0 cannot describe individuals; the statement gives the means and says so. Research findings only: the claim names no signs to look for and no steps to take, which belong to the senior author's emergency guidance (METHODS §8).
